title: What is RAG and Why It Needs a Vector Database

questions.q: What is the 'grounding problem' that RAG solves?
options: LLMs hallucinate confident-sounding facts because they have no access to your private, current documents — fluency is not knowledge
Vector indexes are too slow for LLM context windows
SQL Server cannot store embeddings
LLMs cannot generate fluent text
questions.explain: The chapter defines the grounding problem: models trained on fixed-cutoff public data invent answers about your refund policy or incident reports, so RAG retrieves your actual documents and hands them to the model as context.

questions.q: The chapter states a hard rule: the model used during ingestion and the model used at query time must be identical. How does the schema enforce it?
options: A CHECK constraint on the VECTOR column
A ModelName column filtered in retrieve(), with the query-time model matching the indexed model
A trigger that re-embeds on every insert
It cannot be enforced; it is a documentation convention
questions.explain: The pipeline stores the model name in a ModelName column and filters on it in retrieve(), so vectors from different models never mix in one result set; a VECTOR(n) column also fails loudly on dimension mismatches.

questions.q: VECTOR_DISTANCE returns a distance, not a similarity score. How must results be ordered to get the most similar chunks first?
options: GROUP BY Distance
No ordering is needed — VECTOR_DISTANCE returns ranked rows
ORDER BY Distance DESC
ORDER BY Distance ASC
questions.explain: Because VECTOR_DISTANCE returns distance, ordering ascending puts the smallest distances — the most similar chunks — first; the chapter's exact-search retrieval query uses ORDER BY Distance ascending.

questions.q: Why does production RAG fuse vector search with full-text search instead of relying on semantic search alone?
options: Semantic search is sloppy on exact terms like error numbers, SKUs, and proper nouns — hybrid fusion catches those cases
LLMs cannot read vector results
DiskANN indexes cannot store metadata
Full-text search is faster than vector search
questions.explain: Vector retrieval encodes meaning, not vocabulary, so it misses exact-term matches (error codes, SKUs, proper nouns); the chapter says fusing with full-text (Chapter 11) catches those exact-term cases.

questions.q: What scaling guidance does the chapter give for SQL Server-native RAG versus dedicated engines?
options: Only exact search scales; DiskANN does not
Exact search or modest DiskANN handles up to ~1M chunks; beyond ~10M chunks with aggressive SLAs, evaluate the dedicated engines
SQL Server handles unlimited chunks; dedicated engines are never needed
Move to a dedicated engine past 10,000 chunks
questions.explain: The chapter advises that under ~1 million chunks exact search or a modest DiskANN index is plenty, and to evaluate dedicated engines (Chapters 15–19) only past ~10M chunks with aggressive latency SLAs — keeping chunk store and retrieval shape so migration changes the access path, not the architecture.
